analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal oil-spill response rules: faster water testing, a single response commander, updated contingency plans.
analysis.headline: The oil-spill response bill died in three House subcommittees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the BP Deepwater Horizon disaster, this bill would have forced the federal government to update its oil-spill playbook: water quality testing within 48 hours of a spill, one person in charge (the Coast Guard Commandant) when a spill threatens public health, and a required rewrite of the national response plan every five years, with separate plans for oil spills on land and water [S2][S3]. It was referred to two House committees and three subcommittees in July 2010. None of them ever acted on it. No committee voted on it, no House vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011 [S5][S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial fishermen, tourism businesses, and anyone whose drinking water, beaches, or seafood could be contaminated by an oil spill or hazardous discharge. Faster water testing would tell the public sooner whether local water is safe. A designated National Incident Commander for major spills addresses the confusion over who was in charge during the 2010 BP spill response. Requiring the President to refresh the national contingency plan every five years, with separate plans for land and water spills, would keep response plans from going stale [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to begin monitoring water quality in waters affected by an oil or hazardous-substance discharge no later than 48 hours after the discharge is reported, so residents learn quickly whether their water is contaminated.

Designates the Commandant of the Coast Guard as the National Incident Commander for spills that pose a substantial threat to public health or welfare, creating a single point of accountability in a major spill response.
Requires the President to update the National Contingency Plan at least every five years, including separate response plans for discharges into or upon land and into or upon water.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and other handlers of oil and hazardous substances, which would face updated planning requirements, EPA water monitoring in spill zones, and clear command structure obligations. Taxpayers also indirectly fund the EPA monitoring and Coast Guard response work the bill requires [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill adds planning, monitoring, and reporting obligations for industry and for federal agencies, and those compliance costs fall on oil and hazardous-substance handlers and, indirectly, on taxpayers.

The strongest good-faith objection is that much of what it requires already existed: a National Contingency Plan and Coast Guard-led response framework were already in law, so the bill mainly hardens timelines and names a commander rather than creating new cleanup capability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are modest but real: faster public knowledge about contaminated water after a spill, clearer command in a major disaster, and response plans that don't sit for years without review. The costs are correspondingly modest — some compliance and administrative burden spread across industry and federal agencies. A fair reading is that it was a low-cost, low-drama fix drawn from lessons of the BP spill, not a sweeping reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and three subcommittees in July 2010, but none of them ever held a markup or sent it anywhere, so it died without any vote when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 1, 2010, three months after the BP Deepwater Horizon explosion, and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Natural Resources committees.
Within a week it was sent to three subcommittees: Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, Water Resources and Environment, and Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and expired with the Congress on January 3, 2011.
Support was thin: the sponsor plus 3 of 178 House Republicans cosponsored it, and no Democrats cosponsored.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one won a fight here, because no fight happened: the bill was never marked up or voted on. The parties that would have borne its obligations — oil and gas companies subject to new planning and monitoring requirements — are better off that it never advanced. The House committees that held the bill retained discretion over spill-response legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one acted; oil industry avoided new rules

for.name: Rep. C.W. Bill Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 1, 2010, and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Natural Resources committees.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Democrats did.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill at any stage, so no party-line pattern is recorded. The bill was introduced by a Florida Republican and cosponsored by 3 of 178 House Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed updated contingency planning, EPA water-quality monitoring in spill zones, and command-structure obligations on companies that handle oil and hazardous substances. Offshore drilling's interest in lighter spill-response rules runs against the public's interest in fast, coordinated responses.
These industries absorb the losses when a spill closes fisheries and beaches. Faster water testing and an updated, rehearsed response plan directly protect their livelihoods.

industries.industry: Coast Guard and federal emergency response
industries.note: The bill designates the Coast Guard Commandant as National Incident Commander for the worst spills and builds regular plan updates into the system, locking in the Coast Guard's central role in spill response.
